To share a complex report query that needs no input parameters, choose a {{c1::view}}.
column2:
The view presents the reusable query as a table-like interface.
Review source

column1: For read-only access through an updatable view, grant {{c1::SELECT}} without effective data-modification permissions.
column2:
Defining a view does not automatically make it read-only.
Review source

column1: A view can shield consumers from compatible schema changes by preserving a {{c1::stable output interface}}.
column2:
Adapt the view definition while keeping the columns expected by its callers.
Review source

column1: A view modification that changes several base tables can be implemented with an {{c1::INSTEAD OF trigger}}.
column2:
The trigger performs the required base-table changes instead of the original view operation.
Review source

column1: For an explicitly called order workflow that updates multiple tables in one transaction, choose a {{c1::stored procedure}}.
column2:
Use transaction and error-handling logic rather than assuming a procedure is automatically one atomic transaction.
Review source

column1: Use a stored procedure when the caller needs named {{c1::OUTPUT parameters}} in addition to inputs.
column2:
These parameters can return several values to the caller.
Review source

column1: A stored procedure can both modify permanent data and return {{c1::result sets}} to its caller.
column2:
Use a table-valued function instead when a read-only parameterized result must act as a query's table source.
Review source

column1: To compute a shipping-cost value inside a SELECT list, choose a {{c1::scalar user-defined function}}.
column2:
Weight and destination can be input parameters.
Review source

column1: Return parameterized customer orders directly to a JOIN with a {{c1::table-valued function}}.
column2:
Its result is a table source, unlike an ordinary stored procedure's result set.
Review source

column1: When a parameterized table result needs only one SELECT query, prefer an {{c1::inline table-valued function}}.
column2:
The optimizer can incorporate its logic into the calling query rather than treating it as a procedural result table.
Review source

column1: When a table-valued function needs procedural steps to populate its declared result table, use a {{c1::multi-statement TVF}}.
column2:
TVF means table-valued function. SQL Server, Azure SQL, and Fabric SQL database support this type, unlike Fabric Warehouse.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: To record Salary changes automatically when UPDATE statements modify employee rows, use a {{c1::DML trigger}}.
column2:
The trigger must compare old and new values rather than relying only on UPDATE(Salary).
Review source

column1: For a simple allowed-value rule, prefer a {{c1::CHECK constraint}} over a trigger.
column2:
Use a trigger for required automatic rules that appropriate constraints cannot enforce.
Review source

column1: For explicitly called logic requiring TRY...CATCH and transaction control, choose a {{c1::stored procedure}}.
column2:
A T-SQL UDF does not support TRY...CATCH or independent transaction control.
Review source

column1: On large inputs, a non-inlined scalar UDF in WHERE can add overhead from repeated {{c1::per-row invocations}}.
column2:
This is a performance risk, not a guarantee that every function-based predicate is slow.
Review source

column1: SQL Server 2019 and later can transform eligible T-SQL scalar function calls through {{c1::scalar UDF inlining}}.
column2:
The feature requires compatibility level 150 or higher and must be enabled for an eligible call.
Review source

column1: SQL Server resolves a query and its referenced nonindexed view into {{c1::one execution plan}}.
column2:
That calling query plan can be cached and reused.
Review source

column1: A UDF used in an indexed view expression must be {{c1::deterministic}}.
column2:
The UDF must also be schema-bound and access neither SQL data nor external resources.
Review source
